name: Beginner strength programs (5x5, SS, GZCLP)

lead: Programs such as 5x5 (including StrongLifts), Starting Strength and GZCLP are barbell routines built on a few compound lifts: squat, bench press, overhead press and deadlift. New lifters use them as the usual starting point for building muscle and strength.

The load goes up by a small fixed amount each session or week, which authors say suits novices because they recover fast enough for steady progress, producing rapid early strength gains and then more muscle and better proportions. The programs come from coaches' books and websites; the wider research literature supports progressive resistance training generally, and no trials compare the named programs against each other.

paras: Lifters repeat the same few lifts several times a week and add a little weight each session until progress slows. Starting Strength is from Mark Rippetoe and Lon Kilgore's 2005 book and adds the power clean; GZCLP is a tiered template shared online. Many people follow one for the first months, then move to a split.
Heavy barbell lifting carries the usual resistance-training risks, mainly from poor technique or rapid load increases. No program-specific injury data were identified.

social.title: Fitness for geeks: my annual review of the Stronglifts 5x5 program

angle.text: Beginners follow these barbell programs to add size and strength quickly with a few compound lifts. Small load increases each session drive fast novice gains, which build muscle and improve frame and proportions. They are widely used and come from coaches' books and online templates.

lead: Beginner strength programs are structured barbell routines built on a few compound lifts (squat, bench press, overhead press, deadlift) with the load raised by a small fixed amount each session or week, usually called linear progression. The names most used in lifting and looksmaxxing communities are 5x5 (five sets of five repetitions, including the StrongLifts variant), Starting Strength (SS) and GZCLP, a tiered template shared online.

People use them to build muscle: bigger shoulders, back, chest and legs give a broader, more athletic frame and better posture, which is why they are the usual first recommendation for someone starting to lift for appearance. Starting Strength centres on the squat, deadlift, overhead press, bench press and power clean, with a few assistance exercises such as chin-ups. Its author Mark Rippetoe, a former powerlifter, published the first edition of Starting Strength: Basic Barbell Training with Lon Kilgore in 2005.

The principle behind these programs, progressive overload, is the gradual increase of training stress; Wikipedia traces its formalisation to Thomas Delorme in the 1940s [1]. Controlled trials of the named branded programs against each other have not been found.

paras: Linear progression programs have a new lifter repeat the same few movements several times a week and add weight in small increments. The premise stated by their authors is that an untrained person can recover quickly enough to improve nearly every session for weeks to months.

Starting Strength is organised around full-body barbell lifts with limited assistance work. 5x5 routines, including StrongLifts, use five sets of five repetitions on rotating compound lifts. GZCLP pairs a main lift with higher-repetition secondary and accessory work. Exact set and rep schemes differ between authors and editions and are described in books and websites rather than peer-reviewed papers.

Rippetoe competed in powerlifting from 1979 to 1988, bought a gym in Wichita Falls in 1984 where he tested training methods, and co-authored Starting Strength with Lon Kilgore in 2005. The book went to three editions, and from 2018 the Aasgaard Company began franchising Starting Strength-branded gyms.

The underlying idea of increasing load progressively is often traced to Thomas Delorme, who developed progressive resistance exercise around 1944 while rehabilitating soldiers at a Chicago hospital [1]. A 2011 Hacker News post discussed an annual review of the StrongLifts 5x5 program, which shows the routine's reach beyond gym forums [2].

Resistance training is reported to increase strength and muscle size, and progressive loading is a standard principle [1]. Hypertrophy research describes training volume, intensity and frequency as variables that influence growth. Comparisons of the branded templates with each other have not been published, so claims about which is best come from coaching experience and user reports.

On forums, beginner programs are the default recommendation for adding muscle cheaply with a barbell and rack. Discussion weighs simplicity against variety and compares barbell routines with machine or bodybuilding splits. T Nation members' training logs mention StrongLifts 5x5 and Starting Strength as starting points; one member describes Starting Strength as a perfectly fine program for rank beginners [3][4].

Heavy barbell lifts carry the general injury risks of resistance training, particularly when technique is poor or loads rise faster than ability. Overtraining is described as bringing declining performance and higher illness or injury risk, and periodization is one way of scheduling recovery [1]. Rippetoe is noted for emphasis on coaching lift technique and for a blunt teaching style. No program-specific injury data were found.
No studies found on 5x5, Starting Strength or GZCLP as named programs. General resistance-training and hypertrophy research exists but does not test these templates directly [1].

lore.intro: In fitness and looksmaxxing spaces, 5x5, Starting Strength and GZCLP are the standard beginner choices and are often debated against each other, including on T Nation [3][4].

claims.claim: A simple linear progression program is the fastest way for a novice to get bigger and stronger.
Heavy compound lifts build a better-proportioned physique than machine or isolation work.
Beginners get more from a strength template than from a hypertrophy-specific program.
